From Big Data to Fast Data: Towards High-Quality
Datasets for Machine Learning Applications from
Closed-Loop Data Collection
Philipp Reis, Jacqueline Henle, Stefan Otten and Eric Sax
FZI Research Center for Information Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany
Email:{reis, henle, otten, sax}@fzi.de
Abstract—The increasing capabilities of machine learning
models, such as vision-language and multimodal language mod-
els, are placing growing demands on data in automotive systems
engineering, making the quality and relevance of collected data
enablers for the development and validation of such systems. Tra-
ditional Big Data approaches focus on large-scale data collection
and offline processing, while Smart Data approaches improve
data selection strategies but still rely on centralized and offline
post-processing.
This paper introduces the concept of Fast Data for automotive
systems engineering. The approach shifts data selection and
recording onto the vehicle as the data source. By enabling real-
time, context-aware decisions on whether and which data should
be recorded, data collection can be directly aligned with data
quality objectives and collection strategies within a closed-loop.
This results in datasets with higher relevance, improved coverage
of critical scenarios, and increased information density, while
at the same time reducing irrelevant data and associated costs.
The proposed approach provides a structured foundation for
designing data collection strategies that are aligned with the needs
of modern machine learning algorithms. It supports efficient
data acquisition and contributes to scalable and cost-effective
ML development processes in automotive systems engineering.
Index Terms—Fast Data, Big Data, Data-Centric Artificial
Intelligence, Data Collection
I. INTRODUCTION
Real-world vehicle data is a key enabler for the development
and evaluation of automotive functions. This is particularly
important for machine learning-based systems, whose perfor-
mance and safety depend strongly on the quality, represen-
tativeness, and relevance of the underlying datasets. Conse-
quently, development processes in automotive systems engi-
neering are increasingly shaped by data-driven approaches [1],
in which data collection, curation, and evaluation become
integral parts of the overall systems engineering process [2].
Historically, automotive data collection has largely followed
aBig Dataparadigm, in which large volumes of data are
recorded first and evaluated later in centralized backend in-
frastructures. In this setting, relevant information extraction,
curation, and analytics are predominantly performed offline
after data transmission and storage. However, driving data is
highly uneven in its informational value: common scenarios
are massively overrepresented, while novel, rare, or safety-
critical situations occur only sparsely. As a result, exhaus-
tive recording leads to substantial redundancy, delayed value

extraction, and high storage, transmission, and data handling
costs.
Smart Dataapproaches address this limitation by selecting
and filtering relevant subsets of data based on their estimated
utility. Nevertheless, these approaches still predominantly rely
on centralized, post-hoc evaluation and therefore require large
amounts of data to be recorded and transmitted before their
relevance can be assessed. This maintains long feedback
cycles between data generation, dataset curation, and model
improvement.
To address these limitations, we enhance the concept ofFast
Data[3] for AI systems engineering, shifting data selection
and recording control to the edge, i.e., to the vehicle itself
(cf. Figure 1). In this paradigm, decisions about whether
and how data should be recorded are made at the time of
generation, based on the current system context as well as
predefined collection objectives and strategies [4]. Thus, data
collection becomes part of a closed feedback loop that con-
tinuously aligns observed system behavior with dataset needs.
This reduces the latency between data generation and its use
in model development, while improving resource efficiency by
avoiding the storage, transmission, and processing of irrelevant
data.
The dimensions in Table I characterize how data collection
strategies differ with respect to where and when selection
decisions are taken, how strongly these decisions depend
on the dataset, and how adaptively the collection process is
controlled. In this progression, data collection evolves fromarXiv:2603.29474v1  [eess.SY]  31 Mar 2026

specific and feedback-driven collection. The control strategy
determines whether decisions are taken by static rules, delayed

Together, these dimensions illustrate the transition from
volume-driven to purpose-driven data collection in the Fast
Data paradigm, where data collection is no longer a passive
logging task but an actively controlled procedure.
A. Contribution
Motivated by the shift toward Fast Data, this work in-
vestigates how real-world vehicle data collection can be
aligned with the requirements of high-quality machine learning
datasets. In particular, the following research questions are
addressed:
•RQ1: What characterizes a high-quality dataset in the
context of data collection within the Fast Data paradigm?
•RQ2: Which data collection strategies and architectural
principles enable the acquisition of high-quality data
under Fast Data constraints?
To address these questions, this paper makes four contribu-
tions:
•Derivation of a dataset quality model for Fast Data-driven
data collection, identifying the key quality characteristics
that determine dataset utility in real-world vehicle appli-
cations.
•Analysis of alternative pathways of dataset generation,
showing why selective real-world data collection remains
indispensable despite complementary advances in syn-
thetic and pre-existing data sources.
•Development of a taxonomy of current data collection
strategies by distinguishing data-intrinsic from dataset-
specific triggers and by analyzing their limitations with
respect to dataset quality objectives.
•Formulation of Fast Data collection as a closed-loop,
dataset-state-aware, and structure-aware paradigm, to-
gether with the derivation of the core requirements of
a corresponding collection architecture for high-quality
dataset generation under source-side resource constraints.
II. PROBLEMFORMULATION
In classical knowledge discovery in databases (KDD), data
analysis assumes the existence of a data warehouse from
which a target dataset can be selected and curated offline. In
the Fast Data paradigm for vehicular systems, such a static
warehouse is not available in the same form. Instead, data
emerges continuously as a stream during vehicle operation,

and only a limited fraction of this stream can be recorded,
transmitted, and processed. As a result, the target dataset
is not selected from an already available data repository,
but must be generated through the collection process itself.
This shifts the problem from post-hoc dataset selection to
online data valuation and acquisition. To collect a high-quality
dataset under these conditions, it is necessary to clarify which
dataset quality characteristics are relevant and which collection
strategies are able to realize them under Fast Data constraints.
Accordingly, the problem addressed in this work is how to
generate high-quality machine learning datasets from real-
world vehicular data streams when exhaustive recording is
infeasible. This requires, first, a definition of dataset quality for
data collection, second, an analysis of available methods for
dataset generation and data collection, and third, the derivation
of requirements for Fast Data collection strategies that are
dataset-state-aware and structure-aware.
III. DATASETQUALITY FORDATACOLLECTION
A. Quality of Datasets
The quality of datasets is a safety-critical aspect for the
deployment of Machine Learning (ML) applications in vehicle
systems [5]. Dataset quality is defined in the ISO 52591as:
Definition III.1(Data quality [6]).Characteristic of data
that indicates that the data fulfill the organization’s data
requirements for a specific context.
In [7], [8], data quality is simplified asfitness of use. It refers
to the extent to which the available data are suitable for meet-
ing the needs of a specific task. The evaluation of data quality
is performed at the attribute level using quality characteristics,
which are each assigned to higher-level quality dimensions.
These quality characteristics are quantified through metrics
and describe the data quality within the application context.
B. Quality Dimensions of Datasets
The quality of datasets is not a measurable quantity. A
systematic understanding is required of how quality in datasets

is evaluated (cf. Figure 2). The literature proposes various
dataset evaluation frameworks that analyze datasets from
different perspectives and systematize qualitative dimensions
(cf. Table 2.2 in [8]). A semiotic perspective categorizes the
quality of information and data into syntactic, semantic, and
pragmatic dimensions [9], [10]. A categorization into intrinsic,
contextual, representational, and accessibility dimensions is
described in [11] and further developed in [12]–[14].
In the standards ISO 250122and ISO 5259, data quality is
divided intoinherentandsystem-dependentaspects [6], [15].
The inherent aspect describes the intrinsic potential of data to
fulfill a specific task, while the system-dependent dimension
characterizes the extent to which this potential can be utilized
within a given usage context. The categorization of these
dimensions is also considered in the context of ML and serves
as the foundation of this contribution.
C. Quality Characteristics
The dataset evaluation frameworks structure datasets into
dimensions, which in turn are characterized by dataset char-
acteristics. A dataset quality characteristic is defined as:
Definition III.2(Quality characteristicP).Category of at-
tributes that affects data quality (III.1) [6].
An attribute is a property or characteristic of an (abstract)
object that can be distinguished quantitatively or qualitatively
by human or automated means [6].
In contrast to quality dimensions, dataset quality characteris-
tics are measurable. Their definition serves to quantify dataset
quality through quality metrics. Depending on the evaluation
framework, the quality characteristics differ in terms of granu-
larity, scope, and number of characteristics considered within
the respective categories. The relevance of each characteristic
depends on the considered dimension and the respective phase
in the development life cycle [16].
1) Selection of Relevant Characteristics for Data Collec-
tion:The quality evaluation frameworks described in Table 2.2
in [8]) describe more than 38 quality characteristics whose
definitions, scope, and granularity vary depending on the
evaluation framework and do not follow a unified taxonomy. In
this work, the relevant characteristics are selected using three
filtering criteria (cf. Figure 3).
First, only the inherent characteristics are considered, as dis-
tinguished from system-dependent characteristics in ISO 5259.
Subsequently, a selection is made based on the phases of the

Finally, a distinction is made according to the data collection

diversity, andsimilarityremain.Balancedescribes the distri-

and overrepresentation, which may reduce the performance of
ML models. Trivial duplication of minority classes does not
adequately address this issue and can further impair model
performance [19], [20].Diversitydescribes the degree to
which samples within a dataset differ at the feature level
according to [18]. Low diversity can increase overfitting and
reduce the generalization capability of trained ML mod-
els [21].Relevancedescribes the degree to which a dataset

Similaritydescribes the degree of resemblance between data

of highly similar data points can also promote overfitting of
the ML model. These quality characteristics describe datasets
at a conceptual level. Their evaluation requires numerical
representation throughquality metrics, which map quality
characteristics to measurable values.
D. Quality Metrics
The quality characteristics for data collection introduced
in subsection III-C describe datasets at a conceptual level.
However, their evaluation requires a numerical representation.
Quality metrics map quality characteristics to numerical val-
ues.
Definition III.3(Quality metric).A quality metricQassigns a
numerical value to a datasetDwith respect to a characteristic
P:

For each quality characteristic exists multiple metrics like
the vendi score [22] for deversity or k-nearest neigbourg for
similarity [23]. An evaluation of a different metric and its
impact on Data Quality is still future work.
IV. METHODS FORDATASETGENERATION
The development of ML models is based on datasets that are
used for training. These datasets can originate from real-world

driving recordings or can be generated synthetically through
simulation or generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. In
addition, publicly available datasets exist, which themselves
are based on one of these sources (cf. Figure 4).
A. Real-World Driving Data Collection
Real-world driving data collection records the sensor data
stream from the vehicles surrounding Operational Design Do-
main (ODD) driving environment and is commonly practiced
in industry for testing and validation [24]. In addition to real
environmental, traffic, and vehicle states, phenomena such as
noise and sensor artifacts are recorded, as well as rare events
that occur in reality. With regard to dataset generation, real-
world driving provides the ground truth with respect to the
quality characteristic of accuracy, as it directly represents the
target systems. Consequently, many applications rely on real
driving data [25].
B. Synthetic Data Generation
1) Simulation:Simulation refers to the execution of mathe-
matical models that approximate real-world systems to repro-
duce their behavior under controlled conditions [26]. In the
context of dataset generation, simulation enables the control-
lable, scalable, and reproducible creation of synthetic sensor
data without physical deployment. It comprises sensor, envi-
ronment, dynamics, and behavior simulation, covering aspects
such as sensor modalities, traffic participant interactions, and
environmental conditions (e.g., weather) [27]–[29]. Simulation
supports dataset generation through three key contributions:
dataset augmentation, critical scenario generation, and its use
as a validation environment [30]–[33].
2) Generative AI:Generative AI for synthetic data genera-
tion originated withGenerative Adversarial Networks (GANs),
which were mainly used for image synthesis but suffer from
issues such asmode collapse, limiting data diversity [34]–[36].
More recently, transformer-baseddiffusion modelshave be-
come dominant, enabling controllable data generation through
conditioning (e.g., natural language prompts) [37]–[41]. Sim-
ilar to simulation, they are used for dataset augmentation,
critical scenario generation, and validation.
C. Open Datasets
Open datasets are a key component of data-centric de-
velopment and provide standardized benchmarks for highly
automated driving. They enable the evaluation of methods and
ML models across perception tasks such as lane detection, ob-
ject detection, and semantic segmentation [42]–[46]. Datasets
vary in generation method (real, simulated, generative), sensor
modality (e.g., camera, LiDAR, multimodal), annotation, and
scale. While early datasets were primarily unimodal and
camera-based [47], modern datasets are increasingly multi-
modal, combining multiple sensor types [48]. Beyond per-
ception, current datasets address scenario understanding by
integrating spatial, semantic, physical, and temporal informa-
tion, enabling the evaluation of advanced ML models in tasks
such as visual question answering and decision making [49].TABLE II: Comparison of real-world driving, simulation, and

These datasets are often designed for benchmarking rather than
training, particularly for assessingfoundation models, which
are trained on large-scale, multi-domain data and evaluated
in contexts such as vision-language modeling for automated
driving [49], [50].
D. Challenges in Dataset Generation
The relevance of a dataset always depends on its intended
task and research objective, so dataset generation cannot fol-
low a universal notion of quality but must satisfy application-
specific requirements [25]. For automotive ML, these require-
ments primarily concern diversity, balance, similarity, and
relevance, which must be achieved under the constraints of
theFast Dataparadigm.
ISO 8800 identifies three major factors that limit dataset
suitability:Data Aging Impact,Data Reuse Impact, andData-
Bias Impact[5]. Data aging reduces relevance as traffic
environments evolve, for example, through new vehicle types,
or micro-mobility objects. Data reuse is constrained when
existing datasets differ from the target system, such as in
sensor setup or calibration. Data bias results from insufficient
diversity and imbalance, which is especially critical given the
long-tail nature of real-world driving data [51].
These limitations affect dataset generation methods in dif-
ferent ways. Simulation and generative methods provide con-
trollability, scalability, and reproducibility, but depend on real-
world data for reference or training and remain limited in
realism, sensor fidelity, and the representation of rare anoma-
lies [52], [53]. Public datasets support efficient benchmarking,
but are restricted by aging and reuse effects. Real-world data
collection is more expensive and less controllable, yet it
offers the highest fidelity, captures genuine anomalous events,
and remains essential for both validation and synthetic data
generation.
As a result, no single generation method is sufficient for
high-quality automotive datasets. Instead, public, synthetic,
and real-world data must be combined complementarily.
Within this combination, real-world data remains indispens-
able because it provides the most accurate and current repre-
sentation of the operational domain and is the ground truth for
model training and system validation. Since exhaustive real-
world recording is infeasible due to data volume and long-tail
effects,Fast Datastrategies are required to selectively acquire
samples that most improve relevance, diversity, and balance.

V. ANALYSIS OFDATACOLLECTIONSTRATEGIES
The generation of high-quality datasets from real-world
driving data streams requires the consideration of quality
characteristics and thus a targeted selection of data. A data
collection strategy is defined as:
Definition V .1(Data collection strategy).Let a data stream
S= (x 1, x2, x3, . . .)be given. Then, a data collection strategy
is a functionFthat generates a datasetDfrom the data stream
up to a timeT:
F:S T→ D.(2)
The quality of the data collection strategy is determined
analogously to Definition III.3 asQ: (F(S T),P)→R:
Data collection strategies can be distingushed into data-
intrinsic and dataset-specific selection criteria (cf. Figure 5):
A. Data Intrinsic Trigger
A data-intrinsic trigger functionT Iis a function that maps
a data point from the input spaceΩ Xto a binary outcome,
thereby deciding whether an event is triggered:
TI: ΩX→ {true, false}.(3)
Data-intrinsic triggers operate on patterns in data streams and
can be categorized into three types: (1)rule-based, where
logical conditions are applied to raw signals (e.g., EDR
detecting accidents via thresholds [54]); (2)semantic, where
human-interpretable concepts from model representations or
multimodal embeddings (e.g., detected objects or text-image
alignment) are used for trigger decisions [55]–[60]; and (3)
error-based, where deviations between expected and observed
behavior serve as triggers, either explicitly (e.g., OBD follow-
ing ISO 15031) or implicitly (e.g., shadow mode) [61], [62].
B. Dataset-Specific Triggers
A dataset-specific trigger functionT Devaluates a data point
x∈Ω Xin the context of an existing datasetDand maps it
to a real-valued score:
TD:D ×Ω X→R.(4)Dataset-specific triggers assess data with respect to dataset
properties such as similarity, balance, and diversity. A central
category isanomaly detection, which targets rare or critical
events (e.g., novelties, corner cases, and edge cases) and
addresses the long-tail problem in automated driving [63].
Anomalies can be structured across multiple levels, includ-
ing pixel, object, domain, scene, and scenario, with dedicated
detection methods for each level [64]. Common approaches
include statistical methods, clustering, nearest-neighbor tech-
niques, isolation forest, and classification-based models [65],
which can further be grouped into prediction-, reconstruction-,
generative-, uncertainty-, and feature-based methods [66].
However, not all approaches are suitable for online appli-
cation, highlighting the need for efficient real-time capable
methods.
C. Static and Adaptive Definitions of Normality
A central aspect of dataset-specific collection strategies is
the distinction betweennormalandabnormaldata. However,
the literature defines this distinction inconsistently and at
different levels of abstraction. While anomalies are often
described explicitly, the corresponding notion ofnormality
frequently remains implicit.
In expert-driven approaches,normalis specified manually,
for example through predefined object classes or environmen-
tal conditions [67]–[70]. In machine learning-based anomaly
detection,normalis instead defined implicitly by the training
data [65]. Although this makes normality dataset-conditioned,
it remains static during deployment, since any adaptation
requires offline data acquisition, labeling, retraining, and re-
deployment. Thus, many anomaly-based approaches are only
indirectly dataset-specific: they derive their notion of normality
from a dataset during development, but operate at runtime
with a fixed reference model. In deployment, they therefore
resemble data-intrinsic triggers with respect to the live data
stream.
In addition, these methods mainly address novelty or out-
of-distribution detection and therefore capture deviations from
a learned data distribution rather than broader dataset quality
objectives such as diversity, balance, or similarity.
Overall, the literature spans static expert-defined or static
learned notions of normality. For dataset-specific collection,
this distinction is crucial, since static notions only detect
deviations from a historical reference. However, adaptive
notions enable comparison against the evolving dataset state
in real time. This is a prerequisite for closed-loop Fast Data
collection.
VI. TOWARDSCLOSED-LOOPFASTDATACOLLECTION
Existing data collection strategies only partially satisfy the
requirements of Fast Data. Data-intrinsic triggers support on-
line decisions at the source, but remain limited to local proper-
ties of the current sample. Dataset-specific triggers relate new
observations to previously collected data, but in many current
systems this relation is established only indirectly through
models trained offline on historical data and updated only

in delayed retraining cycles. As a result, many state-of-the-
art approaches are not dataset-specific during deployment, but
merelydataset-conditioned: their decision logic depends on a
historical dataset, while remaining largely fixed at runtime.
This is insufficient when the objective is not simply to
record large volumes of data, but to generate datasets with
specific structural properties. Relevance, diversity, balance,
and coverage are not pointwise properties of isolated samples.
Instead, the utility of a new sample depends on the current
state of the collected dataset and on the gap between this state
and the desired dataset requirements. Fast Data collection must
therefore be formulated as a feedback-driven process in which
collection decisions adapt continuously to the evolving dataset.
A. From Open-Loop Recording to Feedback-Driven Collection
Open-loop collection strategies determine what data to
record using fixed rules or pre-trained decision functions that
do not continuously incorporate feedback from the current
dataset. This principle is typical of Big Data pipelines, where
data are first recorded and stored, and only later evaluated
in centralized infrastructures. Even when anomaly detection
is executed online, the underlying decision function is often
derived offline and remains unchanged during deployment.
Such strategies are inadequate for controlled dataset genera-
tion. First, they cannot account for redundancy, since repeated
observations of frequent situations remain indistinguishable
from genuinely informative samples. Second, they cannot
optimize dataset-level objectives such as diversity, balance, or
similarity, because these are relational properties of the dataset
as a whole. Third, they cannot adapt collection behavior when
the operational domain shifts or when dataset requirements
evolve. Open-loop collection may therefore be sufficient for
event logging, but not for the structure-aware generation of
high-quality machine learning datasets.
B. Formal Model of Closed-Loop Fast Data Collection
To make this dependence explicit, we model Fast Data
collection as a discrete-time feedback process over dataset
state. Letx[k]denote a datapoint from a data streamSat

properties relevant for collection control. The desired dataset

the dataset requirements.
The key quantity is the value of an incoming sample relative
to the current collection objective. We define this value as

In an open-loop or dataset-conditioned strategy,Fis fixed

and thereby changes subsequent collection decisions. Fast Data

cause decisions are evaluated against the target stateθ⋆. An
exemplary implementation is given in [71].
C. Closed-Loop Interpretation
The formal model admits a control-oriented interpretation.
The target stateθ⋆acts as the reference variable, the current
estimate ˆθ[k]is the measured dataset state, and the mismatch

between both defines the current collection need. The policyF
acts as the controller by converting sample value into a
collection action. The exogenous streamSserves as the source
of candidate observations, while the controlled outcome is the
evolution of the retained datasetD[k]. Importantly, the raw
data stream itself is not controlled. What is controlled is the
selection and retention processoperating on that stream. The
closed loop therefore acts on dataset formation rather than on
data generation.
D. Architectural Requirements
The formalization above yields a set of requirements for a
closed-loop Fast Data collection architecture.
1)Explicit target state:The desired dataset properties
must be represented explicitly by a target stateθ⋆,
encoding objectives such as relevance, diversity, or bal-
ance.
2)Online dataset-state estimation:The system must
maintain an updateable estimate ˆθ[k]of the current
dataset state, containing the information needed for
collection control.
3)State- and goal-dependent sample valuation:The
utility of an incoming sample must be evaluated relative
to both the current dataset state ˆθ[k]and the target state
θ⋆, not from the sample alone.
4)Realizable control action:Sample valuation must be
translated into a concrete collection actionu[k], such as
retain, discard, prioritize, or transmit.
5)Recursive feedback update:The selected action must
update the retained dataset and its state estimate, so that
current decisions influence future valuations and the loop
is closed.
6)Online source-side execution under resource con-
straints:The closed loop must operate near the data
source and satisfy Fast Data constraints such as limited
time, bandwidth, storage, and compute.
In this perspective, Fast Data collection is not merely online
filtering. It is a feedback-driven process for steering dataset
formation under explicit objectives and operational constraints.
The key shift is therefore not only temporal, namely moving
decisions closer to the data source, but structural: dataset
generation becomes state-aware, requirement-aware, and con-
tinuously adaptive.
VII. CONCLUSION ANDOUTLOOK
This paper contributed a structured perspective on Fast
Data-driven dataset generation for real-world driving. It intro-
duced a dataset quality model for data collection, compared
alternative dataset generation methods, developed a taxonomy
of current data collection strategies, and showed that existing
approaches are not sufficient for the controlled generation of
high-quality datasets because they lack continuous feedback
with respect to dataset state and dataset structure. Based on
these findings, the paper proposed the Fast Data paradigm as
a closed-loop perspective for dataset collection.The main outcome is a shift from open-loop recording
toward state-aware, structure-aware, and requirement-driven
data collection under source-side constraints. Future work
must now focus on implementing the necessary components of
this paradigm and validating their effectiveness in real-world
driving applications.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces the concept of "Fast Data" for automotive systems engineering, aiming to improve the quality of datasets used for machine learning applications. It contrasts this with traditional "Big Data" and "Smart Data" approaches.

The main points covered are:

*   **Limitations of Big Data and Smart Data:** Big Data relies on massive offline collection and processing, leading to redundancy and high costs. Smart Data improves selection but still requires significant data transmission and offline analysis, resulting in long feedback loops.
*   **Introduction of Fast Data:** This approach shifts data selection and recording to the vehicle itself (the edge). It enables real-time, context-aware decisions on data recording, aligning collection with data quality objectives in a closed-loop system.
*   **Benefits of Fast Data:** This leads to datasets with higher relevance, better coverage of critical scenarios, increased information density, reduced irrelevant data, and lower costs.
*   **Research Questions:** The paper aims to address what constitutes a high-quality dataset in the Fast Data paradigm and what strategies and architectural principles enable its acquisition.
*   **Contributions:** The work proposes a dataset quality model for Fast Data, analyzes data generation pathways, develops a taxonomy of collection strategies, and formulates Fast Data collection as a closed-loop, dataset-state-aware, and structure-aware paradigm.
*   **Problem Formulation:** The core problem is generating high-quality ML datasets from real-world vehicular data streams when exhaustive recording is infeasible, requiring a definition of dataset quality and derivation of Fast Data collection strategies.
*   **Dataset Quality Definition:** The document defines data quality as the characteristic that indicates data fulfills organizational requirements for a specific context, emphasizing fitness for use and the role of quality characteristics, dimensions, metrics, and entities.

structure.title: PROBLEM FORMULATION
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses data collection paradigms in automotive systems engineering, focusing on the transition from "Big Data" to "Fast Data." It highlights the shift from retrospective, backend-driven data collection to real-time, vehicle-centric, and adaptive data acquisition. The main points covered are:

*   **Comparison of Data Collection Paradigms:** A table (TABLE I) compares "Big Data," "Smart Data," and "Fast Data" across dimensions like decision location, selection timing, dataset relation, adaptivity, and control principle.
*   **Evolution of Data Collection:** The document explains how the "Fast Data" paradigm represents a move from volume-driven to purpose-driven data collection, where it becomes an active, controlled procedure rather than passive logging.
*   **Research Motivation and Questions:** The work is motivated by the "Fast Data" shift and aims to align real-world vehicle data collection with the needs of high-quality machine learning datasets. It poses two research questions:
    *   What characterizes a high-quality dataset in the "Fast Data" paradigm?
    *   Which strategies and architectural principles enable high-quality data acquisition under "Fast Data" constraints?
*   **Contributions:** The paper outlines four key contributions:
    *   A dataset quality model for "Fast Data" collection.
    *   Analysis of dataset generation pathways, emphasizing the indispensability of selective real-world data collection.
    *   A taxonomy of data collection strategies based on data-intrinsic and dataset-specific triggers.
    *   Formulation of "Fast Data" collection as a closed-loop, dataset-state-aware, and structure-aware paradigm.
*   **Problem Formulation:** It contrasts classical knowledge discovery with the "Fast Data" paradigm, where data streams continuously and only a fraction can be processed. This necessitates online data valuation and acquisition, shifting the problem from post-hoc selection to generating the target dataset through the collection process itself.
*   **Dataset Quality Definition:** The document defines dataset quality based on ISO standards and literature, emphasizing "fitness of use" and its evaluation through quality characteristics, metrics, and dimensions.
*   **Dataset Quality Model:** A conceptual model (Fig. 2) illustrates the relationship between Dataset, Quality Dimension, Quality Characteristic, Quality Metric, and Datapoint.

nodes.title: Quality of Datasets
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses data collection paradigms in automotive systems engineering, focusing on the shift from "Big Data" to "Fast Data." It highlights the evolution of data collection from passive logging to an actively controlled process driven by the need for high-quality machine learning datasets.

The main points covered are:

*   **Comparison of Data Collection Paradigms:** A table (TABLE I) compares "Big Data," "Smart Data," and "Fast Data" across dimensions like decision location, selection timing, dataset relation, adaptivity, and control principle.
*   **The "Fast Data" Paradigm:** This paradigm emphasizes purpose-driven data collection, moving towards dataset-specific and feedback-driven approaches with real-time decision-making and adaptive control.
*   **Research Questions and Contributions:** The work aims to align real-world vehicle data collection with the requirements of high-quality ML datasets. It poses research questions about characterizing high-quality datasets in the Fast Data context and identifying enabling strategies. The contributions include a dataset quality model for Fast Data, analysis of real-world data collection's indispensability, a taxonomy of data collection strategies, and formulation of Fast Data collection as a closed-loop, state-aware paradigm.
*   **Problem Formulation:** In the Fast Data paradigm for vehicular systems, data is a continuous stream, and only a fraction can be processed. This necessitates generating the target dataset through the collection process itself, shifting the focus from post-hoc selection to online data valuation and acquisition.
*   **Dataset Quality for Data Collection:**
    *   **Definition of Data Quality:** Data quality is defined as the characteristic of data that indicates it fulfills an organization's data requirements for a specific context, often simplified as "fitness for use."
    *   **Quality Dimensions:** Datasets are structured into dimensions, which are characterized by quality characteristics. Various frameworks categorize quality into intrinsic, contextual, representational, accessibility, and system-dependent aspects.
    *   **Quality Characteristics:** These are measurable attributes that affect data quality. The document identifies "relevance," "balance," "diversity," and "similarity" as key characteristics for data collection, explaining their meaning and impact on ML models.
    *   **Quality Metrics:** These are numerical representations of quality characteristics, mapping them to measurable values.
*   **Methods for Dataset Generation:** The document briefly introduces the concept of dataset generation sources, including real data, synthetic data, and simulation.

nodes.title: Quality Dimensions of Datasets
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses criteria for selecting relevant quality characteristics for data collection strategies in the context of machine learning. It highlights various existing dataset evaluation frameworks and categorizations of data quality, including semiotic (syntactic, semantic, pragmatic) and intrinsic/contextual/representational/accessibility dimensions. The document then focuses on quality characteristics, defining them as categories of attributes affecting data quality and emphasizing their measurability. It details a filtering process for selecting relevant characteristics for data collection, prioritizing inherent characteristics influenced by the collection process. The four key quality characteristics identified are relevance, balance, diversity, and similarity, with explanations of their impact on ML model performance. Finally, it introduces quality metrics as numerical representations of these conceptual quality characteristics.

structure.title: DATASET GENERATION METHODS
structure.summary: This partial document discusses criteria for selecting relevant quality characteristics for data collection strategies in machine learning. It outlines various perspectives and frameworks for evaluating datasets, including semiotic, intrinsic, contextual, representational, and accessibility dimensions. The document defines quality characteristics as measurable attributes that affect data quality and highlights the importance of selecting relevant characteristics for data collection. It identifies four key quality characteristics: relevance, balance, diversity, and similarity, and explains their significance in the context of machine learning model performance. The text also delves into different methods for dataset generation, including real-world driving data collection, synthetic data generation through simulation and generative AI, and the use of open datasets. Finally, it addresses challenges in dataset generation, such as data aging, reuse, and bias, and emphasizes the need for a complementary approach combining different data sources to create high-quality automotive datasets.

nodes.title: Real-World Driving Data Collection
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses methods for generating data for autonomous driving systems. It covers three main approaches: real-world driving data collection, synthetic data generation (through simulation and generative AI), and the use of open datasets.

Real-world data collection captures actual sensor streams from vehicles, providing ground truth and capturing rare events, but is expensive and less controllable. Synthetic data generation, using simulation or generative AI models like GANs and diffusion models, offers controllability, scalability, and reproducibility, making it useful for augmenting datasets and generating critical scenarios. Open datasets serve as benchmarks for evaluating machine learning models on various perception tasks.

The document also highlights challenges in dataset generation, including data aging, reuse limitations, and data bias, emphasizing the need for diversity, balance, similarity, and relevance. It concludes that a combination of real-world, synthetic, and open datasets is necessary for high-quality automotive datasets, with real-world data remaining crucial for accuracy and validation, and "Fast Data" strategies being essential for efficient data acquisition.

structure.title: DATA COLLECTION STRATEGIES
structure.summary: The document discusses data collection strategies for generating high-quality datasets, particularly in the context of real-world driving data. It distinguishes between data-intrinsic and dataset-specific selection criteria, with data-intrinsic triggers operating on individual data points and dataset-specific triggers considering the existing dataset. The text further elaborates on static and adaptive definitions of normality, highlighting the limitations of static approaches in capturing evolving dataset requirements. The document then introduces the concept of "Fast Data" collection, advocating for a closed-loop feedback-driven process. This closed-loop system aims to continuously adapt collection decisions based on the evolving dataset state and desired requirements, moving beyond open-loop recording and dataset-conditioned strategies. A formal model for closed-loop Fast Data collection is presented, emphasizing state-awareness and requirement-awareness in collection decisions.

structure.title: FAST DATA COLLECTION AS A CLOSED-LOOP SYSTEM
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the limitations of current data collection methods, particularly in the context of generating datasets with specific structural properties like relevance, diversity, balance, and coverage. It argues that "dataset-conditioned" approaches, which rely on historical data but remain fixed at runtime, are insufficient for this purpose.

The document proposes a shift from "open-loop recording" to "feedback-driven collection." Open-loop strategies use fixed rules or pre-trained functions that don't adapt to the current dataset, leading to issues like redundancy and an inability to optimize dataset-level objectives.

A formal model for "closed-loop fast data collection" is then introduced. This model treats data collection as a discrete-time feedback process. Key components include:
*   **Data Stream (S):** The source of incoming data points.
*   **Feature Embedder (ϕ):** Transforms data points into feature representations.
*   **Dataset State Estimate (ˆθ[k]):** A compact summary of relevant dataset properties at time k.
*   **Target State (θ⋆):** Encodes the desired dataset properties or requirements.
*   **Value Function (V):** Evaluates the utility of an incoming sample in reducing the mismatch between the current dataset state and the target state.
*   **Collection Policy (F):** A function that determines whether to collect a sample (u[k]=1) or discard it (u[k]=0) based on its value.
*   **State Update (E):** How the dataset state estimate is updated based on the current sample.
*   **Collected Dataset (D[k]):** The evolving collection of data points.

The core idea of closed-loop collection is that the collection decisions are "state-aware" (dependent on the current dataset estimate) and "requirement-aware" (evaluated against the target state), allowing for continuous adaptation and optimization of dataset generation.

nodes.title: Closed-Loop Interpretation
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the limitations of current data collection methods, particularly in the context of generating datasets with specific structural properties like relevance, diversity, balance, and coverage. It argues that existing "dataset-conditioned" approaches, which rely on historical data without runtime adaptation, are insufficient.

The document proposes a "Fast Data collection Paradigm" as a closed-loop, feedback-driven system. This paradigm contrasts with "open-loop" strategies by continuously adapting collection decisions to the evolving dataset state and desired requirements.

Key aspects of this closed-loop approach include:

*   **Formal Model:** A discrete-time feedback process is introduced, involving a data stream, feature embeddings, a compact dataset state estimate, and a target state representing dataset requirements.
*   **Sample Valuation:** The value of an incoming sample is determined by its potential to reduce the mismatch between the current dataset state and the target state, considering both the evolving dataset and the requirements.
*   **Policy:** A collection policy uses this sample valuation to decide whether to collect or discard a sample.
*   **State Update:** The dataset state estimate is recursively updated based on collected samples.
*   **Control-Oriented Interpretation:** The process is framed as a control system where the target state is the reference, the dataset state is measured, and the policy acts as the controller.
*   **Architectural Requirements:** The document outlines six essential requirements for a closed-loop Fast Data collection architecture: explicit target state, online dataset-state estimation, state- and goal-dependent sample valuation, realizable control actions, recursive feedback updates, and online source-side execution under resource constraints.

In essence, the document advocates for a shift from simple data recording to a more intelligent, adaptive, and requirement-driven process for dataset generation, emphasizing state-awareness and continuous adaptation.

nodes.title: Architectural Requirements
nodes.summary: This partial document focuses on the architectural requirements for a closed-loop Fast Data collection system. It outlines six key requirements: an explicit target state for dataset properties, online estimation of the current dataset state, sample valuation based on both current and target states, translation of valuation into concrete collection actions, recursive feedback for updating the dataset and its state estimate, and online execution near the data source under resource constraints. The document emphasizes that Fast Data collection is a feedback-driven process for steering dataset formation, moving beyond simple online filtering. It also summarizes the paper's contribution in providing a structured perspective on Fast Data-driven dataset generation, highlighting the shift from open-loop recording to state-aware, structure-aware, and requirement-driven data collection. The conclusion points to future work in implementing and validating these components in real-world applications.

structure.title: REFERENCES
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a "Fast Data" paradigm for dataset collection, emphasizing a closed-loop approach. The main points covered are:

*   **Controlled Dataset Formation:** The core idea is that the selection and retention of data are controlled, not the raw data generation itself. This closed loop focuses on how the dataset is built.
*   **Architectural Requirements for Closed-Loop Collection:** The document outlines six key requirements for such an architecture:
    1.  **Explicit Target State:** Defining desired dataset properties (e.g., relevance, diversity).
    2.  **Online Dataset-State Estimation:** Continuously updating an estimate of the current dataset's state.
    3.  **State- and Goal-Dependent Sample Valuation:** Evaluating incoming data based on its utility relative to both the current and target dataset states.
    4.  **Realizable Control Action:** Translating sample valuation into concrete actions like retaining or discarding data.
    5.  **Recursive Feedback Update:** Ensuring selected actions update the dataset and its state estimate to close the loop.
    6.  **Online Source-Side Execution under Constraints:** Operating near the data source while adhering to limitations like time, bandwidth, and storage.
*   **Shift in Data Collection:** The Fast Data paradigm represents a move from open-loop recording to state-aware, requirement-driven data collection under source-side constraints. This makes dataset generation adaptive and objective-aware.
*   **Contribution and Outlook:** The paper's contribution is a structured perspective on Fast Data-driven dataset generation, highlighting the insufficiency of existing methods due to a lack of continuous feedback. Future work will focus on implementing and validating this paradigm.
